title: A one-sided annual climate test did not resolve a post-2009 runoff loss in south-east Australia
abstract: We test the post-2009 runoff loss without a fitted response curve. We pair years in 2010-2021 with years in 1951-1996 that had no more current or prior rain and no lower temperature. A stable conditional mean that rises with rain and falls with temperature must have a nonnegative expected runoff contrast. We prove the resulting one-sided bound under stated error assumptions. Verified CAMELS-AUS annual tables give 348 AGCD pairs at 73 mainland catchments. The mean runoff contrast is +28.8% of reference mean runoff (conditional 95% limits +21.5 to +62.1). SILO gives 343 pairs at 73 sites and +36.8% (+26.4 to +68.8). The full test thus gives no negative bound. Rain-only contrasts are -17.2% with AGCD (limits below zero) and -11.0% with SILO (limits across zero). The full pairs have about 174 mm more current rain and 162-169 mm more prior rain in later years. Such gaps can hide a real response loss. This result does not show recovery or prove a stable response. Shared weather, source error, omitted climate, selection and conditional interval coverage limit inference. The package includes the proof, source tables, all pairs, code and audits.

display.caption: One-sided runoff contrasts and support by climate ordering. Later years have no less rain in each selected term and, in the full test, no higher temperature. Intervals use shared three-year blocks and spatial cells. Positive contrasts do not rule out a response loss.

citations.reason: Verified annual Q, climate, site membership and coordinates. This study reuses the observations.
Earlier close-climate matching found poor full-climate support. We replace proximity with directional inequalities and derive a one-sided bound.
Model-form dependence of rain-slope loss motivates a test without a fitted runoff curve.
